title: How Can U.S. Special Operations Forces Help Defeat China on Taiwan?
gist: Petit argues the U.S. rotational advisory model for Taiwan is structurally inadequate and should be replaced with a small, permanently stationed special operations cadre modeled on Cold War Detachment A in Berlin — fewer than 100 operators on two-year tours — to make a rapid Chinese victory implausible and complicate Beijing's theory of victory without adding military mass.

themes.theme: The Rotational Advisory Model Is Structurally Broken

insights.claim: Decades of rotational U.S. training teams are useful for specific tactical tasks but poorly suited to the institutional, linguistic, and political work required to prepare a partner for a prolonged campaign against a superior force.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: The gap between advertised U.S. security assistance and actual deterrence value is wider than headline troop or arms-sale numbers suggest.
insights.quote: Military advising for such a complex and consequential situation cannot be treated as a semester abroad.
insights.locator: The United States has spent decades using rotational military teams

insights.claim: The light-footprint posture in Taiwan is deliberate — it signals retractability and registers low on the escalation scale — but it trades away the very expertise needed to achieve the 'harden Taiwan' objective it is racing toward.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: U.S. Taiwan policy contains a self-defeating trade-off: escalation management is being purchased at the cost of defensive capability.
insights.quote: For all those benefits, this method relinquishes the development of true expertise and stymies the very “harden Taiwan” objective that it is racing to achieve.
insights.locator: This posture is intentional

insights.claim: On heel-to-toe rotations the U.S. military operates as an interchangeable-parts model, which makes deployments sustainable but inhibits the development of regional expertise.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Force-generation logic, not strategy, is driving the shape of U.S. presence in the most consequential theater — a structural bias to watch in defense posture debates.
insights.quote: On heel-to-toe rotations to foreign locales, the U.S. military typically operates as an interchangeable parts model.
insights.locator: This operating template does not guarantee forward progress

insights.claim: U.S. military policy toward Taiwan has three components: weapons and munitions packages, menacing naval and air power on the horizon with regional allies drawn into war plans, and light-footprint train-and-advise packages on the island.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: A clean three-part taxonomy for parsing any new Taiwan announcement — arms sale, force posture, or advisory presence — each with different escalation and industrial implications.
insights.quote: First, improve Taiwanese self-defense with weapons and munitions packages.
insights.locator: The Rotational Advisory Problem

insights.claim: U.S. Pacific Command acknowledges defense cooperation with Taiwan but discloses few details about the scale, duration, location, or missions of U.S. personnel, making on-island advisory work the least visible pillar of policy.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Public arms-sale data materially understates U.S. involvement; the unobservable advisory component is where policy change would show up last.
insights.quote: The U.S. Pacific Command acknowledges defense cooperation with Taiwan but discloses few details about the scale, duration, location, or missions U.S. military personnel support.
insights.locator: The U.S. government is open and public about its arms sales

insights.claim: The United States has no treaty obligation to defend Taiwan, and strategic ambiguity leaves Washington in an in-between state of neither committing nor abandoning.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Any Taiwan risk model that assumes automatic U.S. intervention is unanchored — there is no treaty commitment underpinning it.
insights.quote: The United States has no treaty obligation to defend Taiwan.
insights.locator: America’s longstanding policy of strategic ambiguity

themes.theme: The Ukraine Advisory Withdrawal as Cautionary Precedent

insights.claim: The United States conducted a speedy withdrawal of special operations advisors from Ukraine in the months and weeks before Russia's February 2022 invasion, removing personnel precisely when their relationships and expertise became most valuable.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Expect the same pre-crisis evacuation reflex in a Taiwan scenario — advisory presence is the first thing withdrawn, not a durable tripwire.
insights.quote: The withdrawal reduced the risk of direct U.S.-Russian confrontation but also demonstrated the fragility of an advisory model whose personnel could be removed precisely when their relationships and expertise became most valuable.
insights.locator: Clusters of advisors can be easily withdrawn

insights.claim: The $195 billion in U.S. aid to Ukraine came only after Washington gave up the advantage of in-place advisors, meaning the expensive support arrived without the forward eyes and coordinating hands that would have made it more effective.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Cheap pre-conflict presence and expensive post-conflict aid are substitutes with wildly different price tags — a fiscal argument for forward advisory investment.
insights.quote: The $195 billion in U.S. aid provided to Ukraine came after the U.S. relinquished the advantage of in-place advisors.
insights.locator: In Ukraine (2015 to 2022), the U.S. government lacked the imagination

insights.claim: Petit judges that Washington lacked the imagination and political will to prepare advisors to stay behind in Ukraine, and in retrospect they could and should have done exactly that.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: A serving-community argument for accepting direct great-power contact risk — a shift in this norm would be a meaningful escalation-policy signal.
insights.quote: In Ukraine (2015 to 2022), the U.S. government lacked the imagination – and political will – to prepare its advisors to remain behind. In retrospect, they could and should have done exactly that.
insights.locator: In Ukraine (2015 to 2022)

insights.claim: Modest advisor investments in Ukraine from 2015 to 2022 delivered a significant return on investment, alongside Philippine special operations forces and post-2000s NATO partners in Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, Poland, Slovakia, and Romania as evidence small-footprint advising works.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: The empirical case for small-footprint advising rests on cases that stayed out of headlines — success here is invisible by construction.
insights.quote: More recently, modest investments from advisors in Ukraine from 2015 to 2022 provided a significant return on investment for Ukraine.
insights.locator: Too Small

themes.theme: Detachment A Berlin as the Template

insights.claim: Detachment A operated in divided Berlin from 1956 to 1990 with fewer than 100 U.S. Army Special Forces operators on two-year assignments — a precedent for permanent, small, plain-clothed presence inside a contested great-power flashpoint.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Sub-100 personnel is the scale being proposed for Taiwan — cheap enough to be politically feasible, which raises the odds of adoption.
insights.quote: The core of Detachment A was less than 100 U.S. Army Special Forces operators on two-year assignments in the city.
insights.locator: What was Detachment Berlin?

insights.claim: Detachment A was a stay-behind force designed to activate anti-communist sympathizers, cells, and resistance groups to delay Soviet advances and create chaos in the Soviet rear — not to defend fixed positions.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: The proposed Taiwan mission is resistance-enablement, not defense — capability demand skews to comms, sensors, and clandestine logistics, not platforms.
insights.quote: Detachment A was a type of “stay-behind” force, designed to activate anti-communist sympathizers, cells, or resistance groups to delay Soviet advances.
insights.locator: Detachment A was a type of “stay-behind” force

insights.claim: Detachment A teams rehearsed infiltrating man-portable nuclear devices into prospective Soviet-occupied rear areas, illustrating how far stay-behind asymmetry was pushed in practice.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Historical precedent shows stay-behind forces were entrusted with strategic-level effects — a template with far higher escalation ceilings than 'advising' implies.
insights.quote: They rehearsed the infiltration of man-portable nuclear devices into what would be Soviet-occupied rear areas.
insights.locator: Detachment A teams operated on a wide spectrum of tasks

insights.claim: Stay-behind forces force-multiply along three axes — horizontally through people, vertically via munitions, and cognitively through information — a reusable model for asymmetric defense design.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: A clean framework for evaluating any resistance-oriented defense investment: population mobilization, munitions reach, and information effects.
insights.quote: Their method is to force-multiply horizontally through people, vertically via munitions, or cognitively through information.
insights.locator: Backpack nukes behind enemy lines may seem

insights.claim: Detachment A's deterrent value lay not in defeating Soviet forces but in the problem it represented — that even a successful seizure of West Berlin would leave occupation forces facing organized resistance.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Deterrence-by-occupation-cost is the mechanism being imported to Taiwan; it targets Beijing's post-invasion calculus, not the invasion itself.
insights.quote: Its importance lies instead in the problem it represented: even if Soviet forces seized West Berlin, occupation forces would face organized resistance.
insights.locator: Complicating the Adversary’s Theory of Victory

insights.claim: The Berlin analogy is geographic as well as political: West Berlin lay roughly 110 miles inside the Soviet-backed German Democratic Republic, and the U.S. sustained it with a 462-day airlift.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Historical precedent that isolated positions deep inside adversary-controlled space can be sustained — relevant to Taiwan resupply-feasibility debates.
insights.quote: The U.S. responded with the 462-day Berlin Airlift, exhibiting a creative determination to sustain the western sectors of Berlin.
insights.locator: Joseph Stalin attempted to eject Western forces

themes.theme: Detachment Taiwan and Beijing's Theory of Victory

insights.claim: Petit's core proposal is a small enduring advisory cadre permanently in Taiwan, around which rotational teams orbit — changing quality and continuity rather than military mass.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: A policy shift that would be nearly invisible in force-level statistics but materially change the U.S. commitment — hard for markets to price, easy to miss.
insights.quote: Policymakers should seriously consider approving a small, enduring advisory cadre in Taiwan modeled on the organizational principles of Cold War Detachment A in Berlin.
insights.locator: The U.S. advisory model for Taiwan needs an overhaul

insights.claim: Deterrence requires Taiwan to demonstrate it can fight hard and fight long, with the higher-end goal of denying a rapid Chinese victory and animating the prospect of a prolonged, costly campaign.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Duration, not initial defense success, is the deterrence variable — investments in stockpiles, dispersal, and civil resilience matter more than headline platforms.
insights.quote: To successfully deter, Taiwan ought to demonstrate it can fight hard and fight long.
insights.locator: The U.S. advisory model for Taiwan needs an overhaul

insights.claim: Taiwan's one advantage over Cold War Western Europe is that the People's Liberation Army must cross roughly one hundred miles of fitful ocean and fight from beaches to cities to mountains — an opposed amphibious landing being among the hardest operations to conduct.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Amphibious difficulty is the structural brake on a fast Chinese victory — invasion-probability models should weight sealift and beach-assault capacity heavily.
insights.quote: An opposed amphibious landing is one of the most challenging military operations to conduct.
insights.locator: The Russo-Ukrainian War has demonstrated

insights.claim: Taiwan does not need to replicate Ukraine's experience for the comparison to affect Beijing's calculations — it needs only to make credible that an assault leads to prolonged campaign, continued resistance, high losses, and uncertain political control.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Perceived credibility, not actual capability parity, is the deterrence currency — signaling investments can outperform hardware per dollar.
insights.quote: It must credibly demonstrate that an assault would not end with an amphibious lodgment, but could lead to a prolonged campaign, continued resistance, high losses, and uncertain political control.
insights.locator: The Russo-Ukrainian War has demonstrated

insights.claim: The U.S. deterrence scheme for Taiwan rests on three principles — help Taiwan fight its own battle, protect U.S. forces and treaty allies in Japan, the Philippines, and South Korea, and preserve U.S. power to strike a degraded Chinese invasion force at culmination — all of which assume Taiwan can run a protracted war strategy.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: The entire U.S. concept is load-bearing on Taiwanese endurance; if that assumption fails, the fallback is direct intervention or acquiescence.
insights.quote: This approach offers political operating space for U.S. leadership but rests on an assumption that Taiwan can impose costs and operate a protracted war strategy.
insights.locator: In Berlin, the United States concealed an unconventional warfare capability

insights.claim: Taiwan is already building a whole-of-society resilience and defense plan premised on defending itself without the presumption of external support, and is exploring how to activate its population to prevent consolidation of Chinese control after a seizure.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Taipei is planning for a no-rescue scenario — a signal about how Taiwanese leadership actually assesses U.S. reliability.
insights.quote: Taiwan is building a resilience and whole-of-society defense plan. It is preparing to defend itself without the presumption of external support.
insights.locator: Second, this model incentivizes the host

insights.claim: Preparation for population-based resistance must occur in peacetime, not under crisis, which means the window for building it is now rather than at the moment of invasion.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Resistance capacity cannot be surged — the observable buildup (or absence) in 2026-2027 determines the 2030 deterrence picture.
insights.quote: If U.S. advisors are called upon to support this challenging component of strategy, then this preparation must occur in peace, not under crisis.
insights.locator: Taiwan is building a resilience and whole-of-society defense plan

insights.claim: Petit argues a permanent cadre would be less provocative than rotations, not more, because less turnover of personnel means less signature and therefore lower provocation, and the proposal adds no combat capability.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Inverts the standard escalation intuition — a useful counter-frame when assessing whether a U.S. posture change is genuinely destabilizing.
insights.quote: Detachment Taiwan is a shift in persistence and continuity, not in scale. For pure optics, less turnover of personnel means less signature. Less signature means lower provocation.
insights.locator: Too Provocative

insights.claim: If Beijing registers a persistent advisory cadre as a provocation, that reaction would itself be a noteworthy intelligence signal about China's fears and intentions.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Treat Chinese rhetorical intensity over advisory presence as a diagnostic of Beijing's invasion planning sensitivities, not just noise.
insights.quote: If China registers this as a provocation, it would be a noteworthy signal to U.S. strategists in ascertaining China’s fears or intentions.
insights.locator: Too Provocative

insights.claim: The institutional obstacle is the tension between employing forces and generating them: rotational models give special operations commands predictability, manageable timelines, and home-station combat training that a forward-stationed cadre would sacrifice.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Bureaucratic force-generation incentives, not policy, are the likeliest reason this proposal stalls — watch SOCOM's position as the swing factor.
insights.quote: The rotational force model provides clear force readiness benefits: predictability, manageable deployment timelines, and the ability to keep units “fit to fight” with intensive home-station combat training.
insights.locator: Force Readiness

insights.claim: Advisory research converges on three findings: effective advising must occur at the institutional not just tactical level, right-sized long-term efforts produce more enduring impacts, and treating advising as a professional domain rather than a secondary duty maximizes impact.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Evidence-backed criteria for judging whether any new security assistance program is likely to work — apply to Taiwan, Ukraine, or Gulf partner programs alike.
insights.quote: First, effective advising must occur at the institutional level and not just the tactical level; second, advisory efforts that are right-sized and invested with long-term perspectives produce more enduring impacts
insights.locator: Research supports this position

insights.claim: Sobchak's research finding is that consistency in advisor pairing helps produce combat-effective partners, making personnel continuity a measurable driver of partner performance.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: Continuity is the empirically supported lever — cheap to change, and its absence is a concrete red flag in partner-force assessments.
insights.quote: perhaps one of the clearest conclusions … was that consistency in advisor pairing helps produce combat-effective partners
insights.locator: Research supports this position

insights.claim: Petit frames the proposal through George Kennan's particularism — mass cannot be applied everywhere, so America must build custom models attuned to regional problems and local conditions rather than universal templates.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: A reusable strategic filter: prefer bespoke, locally-tuned commitments over scalable universal ones when resources are constrained.
insights.quote: Kennan argued for custom-built models attuned to regional problems, local conditions, and the minute details that seemed small, but loomed large.
insights.locator: Particularism vs. Universalism

insights.claim: Petit's operating principle for forward commitment is to design presence to run deep and stay long, deciding later whether it needs to be withdrawn — reversing the default of building for easy extraction.
insights.speaker: Brian Petit
insights.so_what: A design principle that, if adopted, would make U.S. presence in Taiwan much harder to quietly reverse — a genuine change in commitment credibility.
insights.quote: Design it to run deep and stay long; decide later if it needs to go.
